# A0 validation — 2026-09-12

## Duel extension — 2026-09-14

Package release `2.0.0-alpha.3` adds `a3.duel.1` rules/input/output schemas and separate synthetic vectors. Seven new public tests bring the public suite to 53; with 18 OAuth/GrokBot/MCP regressions, 71 pass under Node 22. All 47 application training regressions pass. The AgentBorn interpreter's 16 tests cover action semantics, full-seed influence, exact budgets, all 1,024 rounds, immutable inputs, output privacy, complete fixture equality and a separate Node worker producing identical canonical bytes.

The independent Python duel oracle verifies six complete gameplay cases and four RNG vectors without importing or inspecting the TypeScript engine; the original seven protocol/training scenario groups also pass. Application and public-package TypeScript, standalone ESM/declarations and scoped lint pass. Historical fixture bytes and match/result/training revisions remain unchanged. See [DUEL.md](DUEL.md) for the exact rules and pending execution binding, journal/issuer and production integration. No sample service, production signer or funded capability is activated.

## Training extension — 2026-09-14

Package release `2.0.0-alpha.2` adds `a0.training.1` evidence without changing historical match/result revision `2.0.0-alpha.1`, its structural schema, or any existing fixture bytes. Nineteen new tests bring the public TypeScript suite to 46. With 18 OAuth/GrokBot regressions, 64 tests pass under Node 22. The Python conformance program adds an independent training group covering exact boundary arithmetic, progress scope, the complete roster and composed hashes; all six previous groups remain passing. Application TypeScript, standalone ESM/declaration build/import and scoped lint pass.

These are content-consistency and pure-policy checks against supplied facts. They do not authenticate completed training, enforce application/signing admission, deploy an on-chain timer, or implement UI/API/MCP. The [training specification](TRAINING.md) states the mandatory A2/A4/A5 verification and activation boundary. Legacy evidence below retains its original date and version.

## Original alpha interface

Revision `2.0.0-alpha.1`. All fixture identities, keys, games, policies and funds are synthetic. No RPC, real wallet, database, deployment or application environment is needed for these checks.

| Check | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Standalone dependency installation from pinned package manifest | Passed; generated package-local lockfile |
| `npm run build` in this directory | Passed; emitted ESM and declarations |
| Emitted ESM import, revision and allocation smoke check | Passed without private application imports |
| `npm test`, Node 24.16.0 | 27 passed |
| `node --import tsx --test test/*.test.ts`, Node 22.18.0 | 27 passed, including final tier/cancellation guards and public verification retrieval |
| `python test/conformance.py`, PyCryptodome 3.23.0 | Six scenario groups passed: played, walkover, cancellation, handler EIP-712, casual signature and studio signature |
| Application-root `npx tsc --noEmit` | Passed with package sources included |
| Scoped ESLint for source, generator and TypeScript tests | Passed |

The TypeScript tests consume checked-in vectors and separately check regeneration consistency. The Python program uses its own canonical encoder, ABI word/dynamic-array construction, EIP-712 digest construction and source-allocation logic. PyCryptodome independently authenticates encrypted fixture bytes and verifies signatures generated by Node. Agreement covers the actual winner/payment outcome ABI, not just an opaque result label.

These checks establish alpha interface consistency and pure validation behavior. They do not establish deployed-contract safety, HTTP server authorization, persistent identity/nonce/exclusivity enforcement, canonical chain inclusion/finality, actual simulation correctness, secrecy of game-specific nested payloads, or successful real-money settlement. Those are explicit later-package acceptance checks in the implementation plan.

On this Windows development machine, Node test execution and the isolated Python dependency required the normal user execution context because the restricted account could not resolve/access installed runtime resources. No application credentials were loaded and no live transactions were sent.
